source.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
source.authors: Yi-He Dong; Lorenzo Noci; M. Khodak; Mufan Li

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares depth scaling in MixiT and a random transformer with different attention initialization and reports task accuracy and hidden-representation covariance. This bears conceptually on V4's initialization and trainable-depth claim, though it does not test the listed initialization methods or plain neural networks.
record.gate_note: The paper's other results concern transformer component ablations and task performance, not the claim versions. No rows are included for those results. The covariance results are reported as evidence of rank collapse, alongside the decimal-addition depth comparison.
record.test_reason: The study uses stable signal propagation to design MixiT and evaluates transformer variants. It does not test V4's activation-matched initialization in plain networks: the models use residual connections and pre-normalization, differ in which components are trainable, and report task accuracy rather than training-speed or training-error comparisons under controlled initialization changes. Representation covariance is a related measure, not trainability itself. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' depth-scaling interpretation: they attribute Random Transformer degradation to signal-propagation problems and representation collapse, and present MixiT as a remedy. This is an attribution rather than an isolated causal test of initialization. Their description of covariance as steadily increasing overstates Table 7, which decreases between eight and 16 layers. The broader conclusion also emphasizes Frozen-QK's induction heads and competitive language modeling, and differing roles of attention and MLPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformer variants with frozen or random attention components and compares task accuracy and representation covariance across depth; it does not use the original initialization methods named in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and attention architecture change the reported decimal-addition accuracy and hidden-representation covariance.

fits_no_version.finding: MixiT achieves 100% decimal-addition accuracy at 2, 8, and 16 layers; the Random Transformer achieves 100%, 23.53%, and 22.88%. Their trainable components and attention mechanisms differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MixiT preserves decimal-addition task performance across these depths better than a transformer with frozen intermediate layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Random Transformer token covariance increases overall from .00218 at two layers to .05438 at 32 layers, with a decrease from eight to 16 layers. MixiT covariance remains between .00088 and .00260.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These transformer variants exhibit different depth-dependent token-representation covariance patterns on Wikitext.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 2.1 establishes a covariance SDE limit for MixiT's attention-only recursion at initialization as depth and width grow jointly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shaped random mixing admits a stable forward-propagation scaling limit under the theorem's assumptions.

record.problems: The depth comparison reports results for only one task and two architectures. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The initialization and depth conditions in V4 are otherwise not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested V4 aspect were identified for extraction.

untested.parts: All: training classification error in convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels and size or regularization effects.
All: spurious local minima and student overparameterization in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
All: depth-related training-error degradation in plain convolutional networks, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the stated initialization exceptions.
All: activation-matched initialization effects on plain-network learning speed and trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian tanh initialization, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
All: learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature dynamics, edge of stability, and divergence.
All: batch-normalization effects on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values match the supplied tables. The original V4 verdicts should be removed: neither transformer task performance nor representation covariance directly tests the specified plain-network initialization claim.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; model size, training duration, and regularization effects.
Teacher-student two-layer ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and effects of student width.
Plain versus residual convolutional networks, depth-related training error, and the stated special initializations or normalization conditions.

The listed activation-matched initializations, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, tanh networks, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks. The study compares only MixiT and a random transformer on decimal addition across depths, and reports covariance for language-modeling representations.
Training above learning-rate stability limits, loss increases, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including the listed datasets and Fixup.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MixiT on decimal addition at 2, 8, and 16 layers
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy is 100% at each tested depth (R1–R3). This supports depth scaling in this specific architecture and task.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Random Transformer on decimal addition at 8 and 16 layers
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy falls to 23.53% and 22.88% (R5–R6), while it is 100% at 2 layers (R4). The study attributes this depth scaling failure to signal propagation challenges and rank collapse.
